title: Diamagnetic and Paramagnetic Substances, and Curie's Law

claims.text: Diamagnetic substances: when placed in an external magnetic field, they get feebly magnetized in the direction OPPOSITE to the magnetizing field (so they are repelled by a magnet). Examples: bismuth, copper, antimony, lead, gold, silver, water. Explanation: an atom acts as a magnetic dipole (each electron orbiting contributes a dipole moment); in a diamagnetic substance the electrons are paired (one clockwise, one anticlockwise), so the two dipole moments cancel and the resultant magnetic moment per atom is zero (M_net=0) with no external field. When a field B is applied, the electrons' motion is perturbed (via the force on each electron) such that the atom develops a net magnetic dipole moment in the direction opposite to B

Properties of diamagnetic substances -- (1) they move from the stronger to the weaker part of an external magnetic field (illustrated with a watch-glass of diamagnetic powder between two magnet poles at unequal separation, piling up in the weaker-field region); (2) when placed in an external magnetic field, they expel field lines -- fewer field lines pass through the material than would pass through the same region in air, so B<B0, mu<mu0, and relative permeability mu_r<1. Superconductors are the most 'exotic' diamagnetic substances: no field lines pass through them at all, so mu_r=0 exactly, which (using mu_r=1+chi_m) gives chi_m=-1

Property (4) of diamagnetic substances: when a diamagnetic sample is freely suspended in a uniform external magnetic field, it aligns itself so that its longest axis is perpendicular to B -- this is its most stable (minimum energy) orientation, since the material 'wants' to expel field lines and minimize the field passing through it; it will not align with its long axis along B

Paramagnetic substances: when placed in an external field, they get feebly magnetized in the SAME direction as B (so they are feebly attracted towards a magnet). Examples: aluminium, chromium, lithium, magnesium, sodium, potassium. Explanation: unlike diamagnetic substances (paired electrons), paramagnetic substances have unpaired (single) electrons, so each individual atom already possesses its own permanent magnetic dipole moment. With no external field, thermal motion randomly orients these atomic dipoles, so the net magnetization M_net=0. When placed in an external field B, the dipoles try to align with B (their own north-to-south dipole direction lining up so that unlike poles face the external magnet's poles), giving a non-zero net magnetization M_net

Curie's law: the intensity of magnetization I of a (paramagnetic) magnetic material is directly proportional to the magnetic field induction B and inversely proportional to absolute temperature T, i.e. I is proportional to B/T. Using B=mu*H (mu roughly constant/treated as such here), this becomes I proportional to H/T, i.e. I/H proportional to 1/T. Since magnetic susceptibility chi_m=I/H, this gives chi_m proportional to 1/T, i.e. chi_m = C/T where C is the Curie constant -- this relation (susceptibility inversely proportional to temperature) is Curie's law

Two graphs following from Curie's law: (1) plotting 1/chi_m (y-axis) against T (x-axis) gives a straight line through the origin (since 1/chi_m = T/C, of the form y=mx); (2) plotting I (y-axis) against H (x-axis) at a fixed temperature gives a straight line through the origin as well (since I=chi_m*H with chi_m constant at fixed T)

markdown_body:
## Diamagnetic, paramagnetic, and (introduced) ferromagnetic substances (NCERT 5.5)

### Diamagnetic substances
When placed in an external magnetic field, diamagnetic substances get feebly magnetized in the direction **opposite** to the magnetizing field (repelled by a magnet). Examples: Bi, Cu, Sb, Pb, Au, Ag, H$_2$O.

**Explanation:** each atom acts as a magnetic dipole (orbiting electrons contribute dipole moments). In a diamagnetic substance the electrons are *paired* — one clockwise, one anticlockwise — so their dipole moments cancel: $M_\text{net}=0$ with no field. When a field $\vec B$ is applied, the perturbed electron motion gives each atom a net dipole moment **opposite** to $\vec B$.

**Properties:**
1. They move from the **stronger** to the **weaker** part of an external field.
2. When placed in a field, they **expel field lines**: $B<B_0 \Rightarrow \mu<\mu_0 \Rightarrow \mu_r<1$. **Superconductors** are the most extreme (exotic) diamagnets — no field lines pass through at all, $\mu_r=0 \Rightarrow \chi_m=-1$ (from $\mu_r=1+\chi_m$).
3. They are **independent of temperature** — since each diamagnetic molecule is not itself a magnetic dipole, random thermal motion doesn't affect the (induced) magnetization.
4. Freely suspended in a uniform field, they align with their **longest axis perpendicular to $B$** (the minimum-energy orientation, since the material "wants" to expel field lines).

### Paramagnetic substances
When placed in an external field, paramagnetic substances get feebly magnetized in the **same** direction as $B$ (feebly attracted). Examples: Al, Cr, Li, Mg, Na, K.

**Explanation:** unlike diamagnetic substances, paramagnetic atoms have *unpaired* electrons, so each atom already has a permanent magnetic dipole moment. With no field, thermal motion randomises these — $M_\text{net}=0$. In a field $\vec B$, the dipoles align with $\vec B$, giving $M_\text{net}\ne0$.

**Properties** (opposite of the diamagnetic case):
1. They move from the **weaker** to the **stronger** part of an external field.
2. Field lines **prefer to pass through** them (rather than being expelled).

### Curie's law
$$I \propto B, \qquad I\propto\frac{1}{T} \quad\Rightarrow\quad I\propto\frac{B}{T}$$
Using $B=\mu H$: $I\propto H/T$, so $I/H \propto 1/T$. Since susceptibility $\chi_m = I/H$:
$$\boxed{\chi_m = \frac{C}{T}}$$
where $C$ is the **Curie constant** — magnetic susceptibility of a paramagnetic material is inversely proportional to absolute temperature.

**Graphs:** $1/\chi_m$ vs. $T$ is a straight line through the origin (slope $1/C$); $I$ vs. $H$ at fixed $T$ is also a straight line through the origin.

---
*Note on this lecture's transcript:* two whole properties sections — diamagnetic property 3 (temperature-independence) and paramagnetic properties 1–2 (weaker→stronger field, field lines preferring to pass through) — are visible on the board but never spoken in the transcript at all, a total-omission gap rather than a timestamp gap. A third graph (I vs. H/T, showing **saturation magnetization** — the real departure from Curie's law at high field/low temperature) is drawn on the board just past where the transcript's own narration stops. All three are grounded from frames alone; see the flagged spans below.
